content: The Council on Chiropractic Education USA (CCE-USA) is an accrediting agency responsible for evaluating and accrediting programs and institutions that offer the Doctor of Chiropractic degree. It operates under the recognition of the U.S. Department of Education and aims to ensure the quality of chiropractic education in the United States. This is achieved through the development of accreditation standards, the promotion of educational improvement, and the dissemination of public information. During the 1920s, there was significant debate between the Universal Chiropractic Association (UCA) and the American Chiropractic Association (ACA) regarding the quality of education within the chiropractic profession. In 1930, these two organizations merged to form the National Chiropractic Association (NCA). By 1935, Dr. John Nugent, a key figure in the development of the Basic Science Board for all healthcare providers, became the first Director of the Committee on Education Standards (CES). Under his leadership, efforts were initiated that eventually led to the establishment of what is now the CCE. Between 1935 and 1940, national chiropractic organizations such as the NCA, the Chiropractic Health Bureau (CHB), and the Council on State Chiropractic Examining Boards (CSCEB) collaborated to improve chiropractic education. The NCA later evolved into the American Chiropractic Association (ACA), while the Chiropractic Health Bureau became the International Chiropractors Association (ICA). In 1938, the CES and CSCEB merged to form a new CES. This committee conducted the first institutional self-study by distributing questionnaires to all 37 chiropractic institutions in the United States that were actively involved in chiropractic education. In 1941, after independent inspections of schools and evaluations of educational criteria, the CES published its first list of institutions with provisional approval, which included 12 institutions. The Council on Education (COE) was subsequently formed by institutional representatives and CES members. On August 4, 1947, the COE received approval and support from the NCA's House of Delegates. Between 1941 and 1961, the Council worked to enhance chiropractic education by merging weaker institutions with stronger ones to create more robust academic programs. Several substandard institutions were closed during this period, reducing the number of chiropractic schools from 37 to 10 by 1961. In 1964, the NCA merged with other groups to form the current ACA, which continued to support the Council on Education. In 1971, the committee was incorporated as the Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE), becoming an autonomous national organization independent of the ACA. It has maintained this status since its inception. In 1974, the CCE was recognized by the U.S. Commissioner of Education and has retained this recognition ever since. In 1975, the CCE became a member of the Council of Specialized Accrediting Agencies. It was also recognized by the Council on Postsecondary Accreditation (COPA) from 1978 to 1992. In 1992, the CCE received continued recognition from the Council on Recognition of Postsecondary Education (CORPA) for a five-year period, which was extended in 1997 until 2002. The CCE is now recognized by CORPA's successor, the Council on Higher Education Accreditation (CHEA).
